opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind memorization sinks is that the way we train language models today kind of guarantees that memorized information gets smeared across the whole network. When a model sees a specific sequence, say a document with someone's personal information, or a copyrighted passage, the gradient updates that help it memorize that sequence land in the same parameters that are also learning general language skills. So by the time you want to unlearn it, the memorized content is entangled with everything else, and if you try to remove it, you end up damaging capabilities you care about. That's why a lot of post-hoc unlearning methods either don't really remove the information, or they degrade the model.

So the shift we're arguing for is: don't treat unlearning as purely a post-hoc problem. Think about it at training time. With memorization sinks, the idea is that you allocate some part of the model, think of it as a set of neurons or units, that are specific to each sequence or document, and those get activated only when that sequence shows up during training. Meanwhile, you have a shared set of parameters that's always active. The intuition is that the shared parameters are under pressure to learn things that generalize across many sequences, because they see everything, while the sequence-specific units become a natural place for the idiosyncratic, memorized stuff to go. They act like a sink that soaks up memorization.

And then at deployment, or whenever you need to unlearn, you can just drop or zero out the sink units associated with the content you want removed. Because the general capabilities mostly live in the shared components, you get much cleaner removal without wrecking the model.

In terms of how training should change in practice, I think there are a few pieces. One is that you need some notion of metadata or identity for your training data. You need to know which document or which source a sequence came from, so you can route it to the right sink. A lot of pretraining pipelines don't really preserve that in a usable way right now. Two, you have to make architectural room for this. It doesn't have to be expensive. You can hash sequences into a set of sink units so you're not literally adding a neuron per document. And three, there's a mindset shift: we should think of the training process as something that can produce models that are structurally amenable to editing later, rather than training first and then trying to perform surgery on a monolithic blob of weights.

What's interesting to me is that this connects to a broader theme. Memorization isn't purely bad. Models memorize partly because some of it is useful, and partly because of the way data is repeated. So rather than trying to eliminate memorization entirely, which would likely hurt performance, you give it a controlled place to live. That's a more realistic goal.

There are still open questions. How well does this scale to frontier-size models and huge corpora? How do you handle content that's duplicated across many documents, where the "memorization" is really spread across many sources? And how do you verify that information was actually removed, as opposed to just being harder to extract? Those are the things I'm excited to keep working on. But I think the high-level lesson is that if we want reliable unlearning, we probably have to design for it from the start.

r001.rationale: The response proposes assigning sequence-specific sink units during training so memorized information is localized and can later be removed by dropping those units.

r002.rationale: It says ordinary training causes memorized information to be smeared across shared parameters and entangled with general capabilities, rather than isolated in specific units.

r003.rationale: It explains that the training setup shapes where information goes: shared parameters are pressured to learn general patterns while sequence-specific units absorb idiosyncratic memorization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I think the core issue is that unlearning as it's usually framed is kind of fighting against the architecture. You train a model on a huge corpus, memorization of specific sequences gets smeared across basically all the parameters, and then somebody comes along later and says "please forget this document" and you're stuck doing gradient ascent on the thing you want to forget and hoping you don't wreck everything else. And empirically, that mostly doesn't work. Either you don't actually remove the information, or you degrade general capabilities, or both. And there's this growing pile of papers showing that so-called unlearned knowledge can be recovered with a little bit of fine-tuning or clever prompting. So the information was never really gone, it was just suppressed.

So the question we started asking was: what if instead of trying to patch this after the fact, you design the training process so that memorization goes somewhere specific? That's the idea behind memorization sinks. The intuition is that you want the model to have a general-purpose set of parameters that learns the shared, generalizable structure of language, the stuff you want to keep, and then you want a separate, designated set of parameters that absorbs the sequence-specific, idiosyncratic details, the verbatim memorization. If you can get that separation to actually happen during pretraining, then unlearning a particular piece of data becomes something closer to a lookup-and-delete operation rather than a delicate optimization problem.

Concretely, the way we think about this is you associate each training sequence, or each document, with some sink parameters. Think of them as sequence-specific neurons or adapters that are only active when that particular piece of data is being trained on. During training, the model has a choice: it can fit a given token either by using the shared parameters or by using the sink. And the key design question is how to set up the optimization so that it only reaches for the sink when the generalizable path isn't enough, which is exactly the memorization case. If you get that right, then the shared parameters learn roughly what they would have anyway, maybe even a bit cleaner, and the stuff that was going to be memorized gets routed into the sink.

Then at unlearning time, if someone asks you to forget document X, you just drop or zero out the sink associated with X. There's no gradient ascent, no retraining, no collateral damage to the rest of the model, because by construction the shared parameters were never the place that memorized that content.

Now, I want to be careful here, because there are a bunch of ways this could fail and we don't have everything figured out. The first is that the separation is never going to be perfectly clean. Some document-specific information will still leak into the shared weights, because the optimization is going to find whatever is easiest, and there's no hard constraint saying it can't. So you need regularization or routing mechanisms that actually push things toward the sink, and you need to measure how much leaks through. The second is scale. If you have a sink per document and you're training on trillions of tokens, you can't literally have trillions of adapters, so you need to think about sharing sinks across groups of related sequences, or having a hashed or hierarchical structure, and then the unlearning granularity gets coarser. The third is that there's a tension with capability. Some of what looks like memorization is actually useful. Models memorizing facts is what makes them knowledgeable. So you don't want to route all factual knowledge into sinks that you're going to throw away. You want to separate the verbatim, copyright-sensitive or privacy-sensitive stuff from genuinely useful world knowledge, and that boundary is fuzzy.

But stepping back, the broader point I'd make is that I think the field has been treating unlearning as a post-hoc problem, and I don't think that's going to work in the long run. The guarantees you can get by editing a model after training are inherently weak. If you want real guarantees about removal, you have to bake the structure into training, so that the question "where does this piece of data live in the model" has an actual answer. Memorization sinks are one attempt at that. There may be better ones. But I think the shift in mindset, from "unlearn after" to "train in a way that makes unlearning tractable," is the thing I'd really want people to take away.

r001.rationale: It proposes designing pretraining to route sequence-specific memorization into designated sink parameters so that the associated sink can later be removed.

r002.rationale: It says ordinary training smears memorized sequences across basically all parameters, rather than isolating them in a specific unit.

r003.rationale: It explains that the optimization setup, regularization, and routing mechanisms determine whether information is directed into sinks or leaks into shared weights.

astra-6.text:
I think the key shift is to treat unlearning as a requirement at training time, rather than something we try to retrofit afterward. If information is spread throughout the model’s parameters, it’s very hard to remove it selectively without affecting other capabilities.

With memorization sinks, the idea would be to give the model a designated place to store information that is specific to individual training examples, while allowing the shared parameters to learn more general patterns. But simply adding that capacity isn’t enough. The training procedure has to encourage the model to use it, and discourage the same information from also being encoded elsewhere.

Then, when you receive a deletion request, you have a more localized target. The important caveat is that removing the sink doesn’t automatically establish that you’ve unlearned the data. You’d want to compare against a model trained without that data and test whether the information remains accessible through other prompts or behaviors.

So I’d frame this as designing training for future deletion. The research question is whether we can make that separation reliable while preserving the benefits of learning from the data in the first place.

r001.rationale: It proposes designing training to place example-specific information in designated sinks and discourage encoding that information elsewhere, enabling more localized deletion.

r002.rationale: It says information can be spread across parameters, but does not state that ordinary training fails to isolate information in individual neurons.

r003.rationale: It says the training procedure should encourage separation, but does not identify the algorithm’s inductive bias as determining whether information becomes disentangled.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key shift is to treat unlearning as something you design for during training, rather than something you try to retrofit afterward. Normally, we train a model to absorb information wherever it helps reduce the loss. That gives us very little control over where a particular piece of information ends up.

With memorization sinks, the idea would be to give the model a designated place to store information that we might later want to remove. You’d want the shared parameters to learn broadly useful patterns, while encouraging more specific memorization to flow into those sinks. Then, when a deletion request comes in, you have a more localized intervention available.

The hard part is making that separation real. Just adding a component and calling it a sink doesn’t mean the same information hasn’t also been learned elsewhere. So the training objective and the way you route information would need to discourage that leakage. And you’d have to evaluate whether removing the sink actually removes the information, while preserving the capabilities you care about. I’d view this as a promising way to make unlearning easier, but not, by itself, a guarantee of unlearning.

r001.rationale: Proposes designing training so specific memorized information flows into designated sinks, making later deletion more localized.

r002.rationale: Says ordinary training gives little control over where information ends up, but does not state that it fails to isolate information in individual neurons.

r003.rationale: Mentions training objectives and routing to discourage leakage, but does not identify the training algorithm’s inductive bias as determining whether information becomes disentangled.
